summary:
Earth Trend Detective System is an end-to-end compliance and intelligence
platform that unifies AI-powered orbital debris risk assessment with multidecadal regional climate trend analysis. The platform automatically ingests
public orbital telemetry (from NASA SPARK, Space-Track, and ESA DISCOS),
executes Debris Assessment Software (DAS) workflows, generates ODAR/EOMP
compliance reports, and computes advanced risk metrics such as DCRA v3 and
the Astro Sweepers Risk Index (ASRI). Concurrently, the system integrates NASA
Giovanni (MERRA-2) Land Surface Temperature (LST) time-series datasets from
2005 to 2025 across major urban regions (Multan, Lahore, Islamabad, and
Karachi), applying Python-based data processing (Pandas, Scikit-Learn) and
linear regression modeling to analyze thermal dynamics, historical peaks, and
anomalous climatic shifts. By bridging space safety with environmental
monitoring through intuitive dashboards and business-ready reports, Earth
Trend Detective System provides operators, researchers, and policymakers with
actionable insights to address both orbital congestion and regional climate
change.
details:
1. Executive Summary, Objectives & Project Scope

Project overview:

Astro Sweepers, also named the Earth Trend Detective System, is presented as an integrated platform for orbital-debris compliance and regional climate risk intelligence. The project description combines public orbital information, including Space-Track TLEs/CDMs and ESA DISCOS data, with landsurface-temperature (LST)time-series information obtained through NASA Giovanni using MERRA-2 data for the 2005–2025 period.

Core value proposition:

The platform is intended to allow space operators to submit satellite orbital information for collision-risk and compliance assessment. It also provides temperature-trend information for selected urban areas to support environmental monitoring and further predictive analysis.

1.1 Project Objectives

• Develop a risk-intelligence workflow that evaluates orbital objects using the

project’s DCRA v3 scoring approach.

• Assess end-of-life compliance scenarios using the described v-integrated ∆

compliance model and DAS-related risk

adjustment.

• Support object selection while seeking fair representation across the listed

countries and regions.

• Organize orbital information for the proposed ODAR/EOMP reporting workflow.

• Analyze annual LST trends for Multan, Lahore, Islamabad, and Karachi from

2005 to 2025.

• Present long-term debris-population scenarios and connect the project direction

with space sustainability and

climate-related goals

1.2 Project Scope

The scope described in the supplied material has two connected areas. The spacesystems area covers orbital data intake, risk scoring, compliance assessment, object selection, reporting automation, a satellite case study, and population simulations. The climate-analysis area covers annual average LST values for four cities over 21 years, statistical summaries, and linear-regression trend estimates. The report also documents proposed machine-learning extensions and a subscription/licensing business model.

Scope boundary:

The supplied material does not provide a complete software architecture, user-interface specification, detailed implementation code, full DCRA weighting coefficients, or raw annual climate observations. These are therefore not invented in this report.

2. Methodology and System Workflow

This section organizes the process already described in the project material into a clear sequence. It explains the intended flow without claiming additional implementation steps that were not supplied.

2.1 Orbital Debris and Compliance Workflow

2.2 Climate Data and Analysis Workflow

2.3 Tools and Technologies

3. Core Technical Innovations & Algorithms (Space Systems)

3.1 DCRA v3 Risk Scoring

DCRA v3 is described as a physics-based scoring method intended to approximate the collision risk of an object before the DAS stage.

It combines four weighted components:

• D — Debris Legacy: considers the object’s age and type, such as rocket body, debris or payload.

• C — Compliance: uses indicators related to end-of-life rules, including

perigee altitude, age and debris flag.

• R — Risk Burden: considers a two-dimensional Gaussian-smoothed

altitude–inclination density map, eccentricity and radar cross-section (size).

• S — Sustainability Alignment: considers perigee feasibility and

eccentricity.

The original project material identifies these four weighted components but does

not provide their individual numerical weights or a complete expanded DCRA

equation. The report therefore preserves the component definitions without

creating missing coefficients.

3.2 v-Integrated Compliance Model

The model calculates a single-burn change in velocity ( v) to lower an object's ∆ perigee toward a target altitude of 120 km or 550 km. The stated purpose is to assess the resulting orbital lifetime and casualty-compliance status.

Supplied relationship:

DCRAWITH DAS = DCRABASE × (1 - DASREDUCTION)

In this expression, DCRABASE is the baseline score and DASREDUCTION is the

reduction factor used by the project. The result is the DCRA value after applying

the stated DAS reduction.

3.3 Selection Algorithms & Fair Representation

The project selects the Top 5 objects according to DCRA. It also seeks representation of up to three objects per listed country or region—U.S., Russia, China, India, ESA/EU and others—to reduce the possibility that the selection is dominated by one constellation or country group.

3.4 ODAR/EOMP Automation

The proposed automation fills NASA's ODAR and EOMP templates using OMM data, TLE orbital information and v plans. This is intended to reduce manual ∆ reporting effort and organize compliance information in a consistent format.

4. Regional Climate & Land Surface Temperature (LST) Trend Analysis (2005–2025)

The climate analysis uses NASA Giovanni (MERRA-2) time-series data as described in the supplied project material. Pandas, NumPy, Scikit-Learn and Matplotlib/Seaborn are identified as the processing, analysis and visualization tools. Annual average temperatures are reported in Kelvin (K) for four cities over 20 years.

4.1 Trend Behaviour and Analytical Insights

The supplied regression results show negative slopes for all four cities. Within the project’s analysis, this indicates a slight downward linear trend over the study period rather than a continuously increasing annual series. A negative slope describes the fitted trend; it does not mean that every individual year was cooler than the previous year

GRAPH:

Reported temperature peaks:

Prominent increases are reported in 2009, 2016 and 2018. Lahore reached

approximately 299.8 K in 2009; Multan and Islamabad reached their reported

peaks in 2016; and Karachi reached 301.68 K in 2018.

The original project description proposes regional heatwaves, severe summer

anomalies, El Niño-related meteorological cycles and urban heat-island effects as

possible explanations. These are presented as proposed explanations, not as

causes proven by the supplied analysis.

Reported temperature decreases:

A synchronized drop is reported in 2020 across all four cities, with secondary dips around 2022–2023. The supplied project description proposes regional meteorological shifts, increased precipitation, persistent cloud cover and regional cooling anomalies as possible explanations. These explanations have not been independently tested in this report


4.2 City-Specific Statistical Summaries

The table summarizes the statistics provided in the original project report. Standard deviation describes the spread of annual values around the mean. Minimum and maximum entries include the years reported in the source material.

5. Case Studies & Population Simulations ( 2025–2100)

5.1 Satellite Case Study: China-1 CZ 2C R/B

The case study describes the China-1 CZ 2C rocket body at an altitude of 613 × 671 km, with an inclination of 98.4° and an age greater than 11 years. In the baseline scenario without DAS, the reported orbital lifetime is greater than 100 years and the risk is described as high. The project then considers lowering perigee to 550 km using v = 22 m/s. The supplied result states that this scenario meets the 25- ∆ year rule and reduces casualty area.

5.2 Long-Term Population Simulation (2025–2100)

The simulation is described as covering 21,800 objects larger than 10 cm. Three scenarios are compared: no DAS,DAS applied in 2025 only, and DAS combined with ASRI through 2100.

The probability notation is typeset here with readable negative exponents. The numerical values are transcribed from the supplied project information and have not been recalculated or independently verified.

6. Strategic Roadmap & Future Machine Learning Expansion

• Physics-Informed Models: Neural networks to model orbital dynamics

and atmospheric drag under changing solar

cycles.

• Conjunction Prediction GNNs: Graph neural networks to anticipate

multi-body interactions and possible cascade

collision risks.

• Material & Mass Classification: Computer vision using radar/optical data

to support salvage and recycling

identification.

• Insurance & Pricing AI: Use ASRI scores to estimate claim likelihood and

support dynamic insurance premiums.

• Debris Removal Robotics: Reinforcement-learning algorithms for

controlling small debris-removal sweepers. These items are presented as future

expansion directions in the project description, not as features confirmed to be

fully implemented.

7. LEO Sustainability, UN Alignment & SDGs

7.1 Continuous ASRI Monitoring

The project proposes a publicly accessible dashboard that updates ASRI information weekly for regulators and space operators. This is intended to make risk information easier to monitor and share.

7.2 Open Data Sharing

The project proposes an international data-sharing framework under UNOOSA to improve access to TLE, CDM and material datasets. This is a proposed framework in the project description; it should not be read as an already adopted UNOOSA system.

7.3 Alignment with the UN Sustainable

Development Goals

SDG 9 — Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure: The project’s

proposed data platform, risk-assessment methods and machine-learning

roadmap relate to innovation and technology development.

SDG 13 — Climate Action: The regional LST analysis supports the project’s

environmental-monitoring focus by examining temperature patterns across

selected cities.

The project also discusses long-term orbital sustainability. UNOOSA’s Long-term

Sustainability Guidelines provide an international reference framework for safe

and sustainable space activities. The project’s proposed monitoring and datasharing ideas can be discussed in relation to these guidelines, but this report does

not claim formal endorsement or certification.

8. Business Model, Profitability & Financial Projections

8.1 SaaS Core and Subscription Tiers

The proposed software-as-a-service model includes four subscription tiers: Lite,

Compliance Pack, Pro and Monitor. The project description targets recurring

revenue and an 80% gross margin. It lists indicative pricing of $300–$1,200 per

month for small operators and $50,000–$150,000 per year for large constellations.

8.2 Licensing and Partnerships

The project proposes licenses for satellite operators and insurers. These licenses

would allow risk scores to be integrated into operational planning workflows and

insurance underwriting processes.

8.3 Financial Viability

The supplied project description states that audited IFRS statements for 2025–

2028 indicate break-even within 60 missions, followed by growth toward

commercial viability. The underlying financial statements, assumptions and

calculations were not included in the material used to prepare this report; this

statement is therefore reproduced as a project-provided claim and is not

independently confirmed here.

9. Conclusion, Limitations & Future

Scope

9.1 Conclusion

The Earth Trend Detective System brings together two project themes: orbitaldebris risk and compliance analysis, and regional land-surface-temperature trend

analysis. Its space-systems concept uses DCRA v3 scoring, a v-integrated ∆

compliance approach, object-selection rules and proposed ODAR/EOMP reporting

automation. Its climate-analysis component examines annual LST data for

Multan, Lahore, Islamabad and Karachi from 2005 to 2025 using statistical

summaries and linear regression.

The supplied results report negative regression slopes for all four cities, with

different peak years and a shared reported low in 2020. The space-debris case

study and population scenarios describe how the proposed DAS and ASRI

approaches may reduce orbital lifetime and risk indicators. The roadmap extends

the concept through machine learning, monitoring, data sharing and a

subscription/licensing model.

Overall, the project presents an integrated technical concept connecting orbital

sustainability with environmental data analysis. Its next development stage

should focus on transparent methodology, reproducible calculations, validation

of input datasets, and clear evidence for simulation and financial claims.

9.2 Limitations and Items Requiring Verification

• The complete DCRA v3 equation and the numerical weights for D, C, R and S

were not included in the supplied report.

• Raw annual LST observations and the full data-cleaning procedure were not

included, so the reported means, standard deviations and slopes could not be

recomputed here.

• The proposed reasons for temperature peaks and drops are explanations from

the supplied project text; causal testing was not provided.

• The satellite case study and population simulation values were retained as

supplied and were not independently reproduced.

• The financial statement concerning audited IFRS projections and break-even

within 60 missions requires supporting statements and calculation details.

• The project material names “NASA SPARK 2022.” The SPARK 2022 dataset page

located for the references identifies the dataset with CVI² / University of

Luxembourg and its related Zenodo publication. Confirm the exact dataset and

attribution before final academic submission.

• The exact source file/version and parameter selection for the climate data

should be recorded so another researchercan reproduce the four-city analysis.

9.3 Future Scope

• Publish the complete DCRA equation, component weights and scoring ranges.

• Document the climate dataset variable, spatial extraction method, time

aggregation and missing-value handling.

• Re-run the climate analysis from the raw annual data and compare the results

with the reported summary table.

• Validate orbital case-study and population-simulation outputs with documented

input assumptions.

• Provide supporting financial assumptions and audited statements for the

business projections.

• Add the actual project graphs, with figure numbers, captions, axis labels, units

and source notes, in a later version of the report.

10. References and Documentation Links

The references below are grouped by the part of the project they can support.

Keep a source in the final bibliography only when the team actually used it or

directly relied on it. Record the exact product/version and access date where

applicable.
